problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:**  
I have successfully solved the problem. The minimum number of tiles required is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Structure of the uncovered squares.**  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares is a permutation matrix: there exists a permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (with \(n=2025\)) such that the uncovered squares are \((i,\sigma(i))\) for \(i=1,\dots ,n\).

2. **Lower bound \(2n-2\).**  
   For each row \(i\) define the left‑adjacent square  
   \[
   L_i=(i,\sigma(i)-1)\quad\text{if }\sigma(i)>1,
   \]
   and the right‑adjacent square  
   \[
   R_i=(i,\sigma(i)+1)\quad\text{if }\sigma(i)<n.
   \]
   Exactly one row has \(\sigma(i)=1\) and one row has \(\sigma(i)=n\); consequently there are \(n-1\) defined left squares and \(n-1\) defined right squares, altogether \(2n-2\) distinct squares.  

   **Claim.** No axis‑parallel rectangular tile can contain two distinct squares among the collection \(\{L_i,R_i\}\).  
   *Proof.*  
   – If a tile contained two left squares \(L_i\) and \(L_j\) (with \(i\neq j\)), its column interval would contain both columns \(\sigma(i)-1\) and \(\sigma(j)-1\). Since \(\sigma(i)\neq\sigma(j)\), that interval must also contain at least one of the columns \(\sigma(i)\) or \(\sigma(j)\); together with the corresponding row it would contain a hole, contradicting the requirement that holes stay uncovered.  
   – The same argument applies to two right squares.  
   – If a tile contained a left square \(L_i\) and a right square \(R_j\), its column interval would contain both \(\sigma(i)-1\) and \(\sigma(j)+1\); consequently it would also contain at least one of the columns \(\sigma(i)\) or \(\sigma(j)\), again forcing the tile to cover a hole. ∎  

   Since each of the \(2n-2\) squares must be covered and no tile can cover two of them, any admissible tiling uses at least \(2n-2\) tiles.

3. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   Choose the identity permutation \(\sigma(i)=i\); the uncovered squares are the diagonal squares \((i,i)\).  

   For each column \(j\) with \(1\le j\le n-1\) place a vertical tile covering the squares  
   \[
   T^{\text{down}}_j=\{(i,j)\mid i=j+1,\dots ,n\},
   \]
   a rectangle of size \((n-j)\times1\).  

   For each column \(j\) with \(2\le j\le n\) place a vertical tile covering the squares  
   \[
   T^{\text{up}}_j=\{(i,j)\mid i=1,\dots ,j-1\},
   \]
   a rectangle of size \((j-1)\times1\).  

   These \( (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) tiles are pairwise disjoint, they cover every non‑diagonal square, and the only uncovered squares are the diagonal ones, one per row and one per column.  

   Because the construction meets the lower bound, the bound is tight and the minimum number of tiles equals \(2n-2\). For \(n=2025\) this gives \(2\cdot2025-2=4048\).

---

### Detailed Solution ###

Let \(n=2025\).  
A placement of rectangular tiles satisfying the condition must leave exactly one uncovered unit square in each row and each column. Hence there exists a permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that the set of uncovered squares is  

\[
U=\{(i,\sigma(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}.
\tag{1}
\]

All other squares  

\[
C=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le n,\;j\neq\sigma(i)\}
\tag{2}
\]

must be covered by axis‑parallel rectangles whose interiors are pairwise disjoint.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  A universal lower bound

For each row \(i\) define  

\[
L_i=
\begin{cases}
(i,\sigma(i)-1), & \text{if }\sigma(i)>1,\\[2mm]
\text{undefined}, & \text{if }\sigma(i)=1,
\end{cases}
\qquad
R_i=
\begin{cases}
(i,\sigma(i)+1), & \text{if }\sigma(i)<n,\\[2mm]
\text{undefined}, & \text{if }\sigma(i)=n .
\end{cases}
\tag{3}
\]

The squares \(L_i\) lie immediately to the left of the hole in row \(i\); the squares \(R_i\) lie immediately to the right.  
Since \(\sigma\) is a bijection, the columns \(\sigma(i)-1\) (for those \(i\) with \(\sigma(i)>1\)) are all distinct, and likewise the columns \(\sigma(i)+1\) (for those \(i\) with \(\sigma(i)<n\)) are all distinct.  
Exactly one row has \(\sigma(i)=1\) and exactly one row has \(\sigma(i)=n\); therefore the total number of defined squares among the \(L_i\) and \(R_i\) is  

\[
| \{L_i\}|+| \{R_i\}| = (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
\tag{4}
\]

All these squares belong to the set \(C\) and must be covered by tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Claim.** No tile can contain two distinct squares from the collection \(\{L_i,R_i\}\).

*Proof.*  
Consider a rectangular tile \(T\) whose set of covered unit squares is a Cartesian product of a row interval \([a,b]\) and a column interval \([c,d]\) (with \(a\le b\) and \(c\le d\)).  

*Two left squares.*  
Suppose \(T\) contains \(L_i=(i,\sigma(i)-1)\) and \(L_j=(j,\sigma(j)-1)\) with \(i\neq j\). Then \(c\le\sigma(i)-1\le d\) and \(c\le\sigma(j)-1\le d\); hence the column interval \([c,d]\) contains both columns \(\sigma(i)-1\) and \(\sigma(j)-1\). Because \(\sigma(i)\neq\sigma(j)\), the interval \([c,d]\) must also contain at least one of the columns \(\sigma(i)\) or \(\sigma(j)\). Consequently, together with the rows \(i\) or \(j\) (which lie in \([a,b]\) because the corresponding squares are in \(T\)), the tile would contain the hole \((i,\sigma(i))\) or \((j,\sigma(j))\), contradicting the requirement that holes stay uncovered.

*Two right squares.*  
The same argument applies to two right squares \(R_i,R_j\), using the columns \(\sigma(i)+1,\sigma(j)+1\).

*One left and one right square.*  
Assume \(T\) contains \(L_i=(i,\sigma(i)-1)\) and \(R_j=(j,\sigma(j)+1)\). Then \([c,d]\) contains both \(\sigma(i)-1\) and \(\sigma(j)+1\). Hence it also contains at least one of the columns \(\sigma(i)\) or \(\sigma(j)\) (the interval between \(\sigma(i)-1\) and \(\sigma(j)+1\) necessarily passes through either \(\sigma(i)\) or \(\sigma(j)\)). Consequently \(T\) would contain the hole \((i,\sigma(i))\) or \((j,\sigma(j))\), again a contradiction. ∎

Because each of the \(2n-2\) squares in (4) must be covered and no tile can cover two of them, any admissible tiling uses at least \(2n-2\) tiles:

\[
\boxed{\text{any valid tiling requires at least }2n-2\text{ tiles}.}
\tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  A tiling with exactly \(2n-2\) tiles

Choose the identity permutation \(\sigma(i)=i\) for all \(i\). Then the uncovered squares are the diagonal squares  

\[
U=\{(i,i)\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}.
\tag{6}
\]

For each column \(j\) with \(1\le j\le n-1\) place the vertical tile  

\[
T^{\text{down}}_j=\{(i,j)\mid i=j+1,\dots ,n\},
\tag{7}
\]
which is a rectangle of dimensions \((n-j)\times1\).

For each column \(j\) with \(2\le j\le n\) place the vertical tile  

\[
T^{\text{up}}_j=\{(i,j)\mid i=1,\dots ,j-1\},
\tag{8}
\]
which is a rectangle of dimensions \((j-1)\times1\).

*Verification.*  

*Disjointness.*  
In a fixed column \(j\) the two tiles occupy the row intervals \([1,j-1]\) and \([j+1,n]\), which are separated by the single uncovered square \((j,j)\); thus they do not intersect. Tiles belonging to different columns lie in distinct columns, so all tiles are pairwise disjoint.

*Coverage of non‑diagonal squares.*  
Let \((i,j)\) be a square with \(i\neq j\).  
If \(i<j\) then \(i\le j-1\), so \((i,j)\in T^{\text{up}}_j\).  
If \(i>j\) then \(i\ge j+1\), so \((i,j)\in T^{\text{down}}_j\).  
Hence every off‑diagonal square is covered by exactly one tile.

*Uncovered squares.*  
The only squares not belonging to any tile are the diagonal squares \((i,i)\) for \(i=1,\dots ,n\). Consequently each row and each column contains exactly one uncovered square, as required.

The total number of tiles is  

\[
| \{T^{\text{down}}_j\mid 1\le j\le n-1\}|+| \{T^{\text{up}}_j\mid 2\le j\le n\}|=(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
\tag{9}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  Minimality

From (5) we have a universal lower bound of \(2n-2\) tiles.  
From (9) we have an explicit tiling that uses exactly \(2n-2\) tiles.  
Therefore the bound is tight, and the minimum possible number of tiles equals \(2n-2\).

For the given grid size \(n=2025\),

\[
2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4050-2 = 4048 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4048}
\]
